claim: Lobule HVI of the cerebellar cortex and its downstream target, the interposed nucleus (IpN), are essential for the manifestation of conditioned eyelid behavior.
source: Lobule HVI of the cerebellar cortex and its downstream target, the interposed nucleus (IpN), are essential for the manifestation of this conditioned eyelid behavior (McCormick et al., 1982; McCormick and Thompson, 1984; Yeo et al., 1985a1985, 1985b; Clark et al., 1992; Krupa and Thompson, 1997; Ohyama et al., 2006; Mostofi et al., 2010; Heiney et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: The expression of CRs may require plasticity at the excitatory parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse.
source: Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of cerebellar cortical Purkinje cells indicate that the expression of CRs may require various cell physiological processes, including plasticity at the excitatory parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse (Ito and Kano, 1982; Koekkoek et al., 2003; Schonewille et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies involving genetic and pharmacological manipulations.

claim: The expression of CRs may require inhibition at the molecular layer interneuron to Purkinje cell synapse.
source: Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of cerebellar cortical Purkinje cells indicate that the expression of CRs may require various cell physiological processes, including plasticity at the excitatory parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse (Ito and Kano, 1982; Koekkoek et al., 2003; Schonewille et al., 2010), inhibition at the molecular layer interneuron to Purkinje cell synapse (ten Brinke et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on inhibition at this synapse.

claim: The expression of CRs may require intrinsic mGluR7-mediated processes in Purkinje cells.
source: Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of cerebellar cortical Purkinje cells indicate that the expression of CRs may require various cell physiological processes, including plasticity at the excitatory parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse (Ito and Kano, 1982; Koekkoek et al., 2003; Schonewille et al., 2010), inhibition at the molecular layer interneuron to Purkinje cell synapse (ten Brinke et al., 2015), as well as intrinsic mGluR7-mediated processes in Purkinje cells (Johansson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on mGluR7-mediated processes.

claim: IpN neurons that can drive eyeblink behavior through the red nucleus and facial nucleus provide a feedback to the cerebellar cortex that amplifies the CR.
source: IpN neurons that can drive eyeblink behavior through the red nucleus and facial nucleus provide a feedback to the cerebellar cortex that amplifies the CR (Gao et al., 2016; Giovannucci et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this feedback mechanism.

claim: IpN neurons receive excitatory inputs from mossy fiber and climbing fiber collaterals.
source: Moreover, IpN neurons receive excitatory inputs from mossy fiber and climbing fiber collaterals, which need to be integrated with the inhibitory inputs from the Purkinje cells and local interneurons and possibly even from recurrent collaterals of the nucleo-olivary neurons (Chan-Palay, 1973, Chan-Palay, 1977; de Zeeuw et al., 1988, 1997; Van der Want et al., 1989; Uusisaari et al., 2007; Uusisaari and Knöpfel, 2008, 2011, 2012; Bagnall et al., 2009; Kodama et al., 2012; Witter et al., 2013; Boele et al., 2013; Najac and Raman, 2015; Canto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: 270 recordings of IpN cells were initially collected that were located below Purkinje cell layers at depths between 1500–3000 μm.
source: Initially, we collected 270 recordings of IpN cells that were located below Purkinje cell layers at depths between 1500–3000 μm (Figure 1B), that were recorded during at least 10 valid CS-US trials, ánd that showed modulation in their firing rate in response to the CS and/or US.
evidence: The claim describes the data collection methodology and criteria used in the study.

claim: Firing frequency of IpN cells averaged 67 ± 27 Hz.
source: Firing frequency was similar along the depth of the IpN (r = 0.085, p=0.16, n = 270, Pearson), averaging 67 ± 27 Hz.
evidence: The claim reports a measured average firing frequency with statistical details.

claim: 60 cells showed at least 5 Hz facilitation in the CS-US interval (22.2%).
source: Within the entire dataset, 60 cells showed at least 5 Hz facilitation in the CS-US interval (22.2%, Figure 1C,F,I)
evidence: The claim reports a specific count and percentage of cells showing facilitation, with reference to figure panels.

claim: 23 cells showed at least 5 Hz suppression in the CS-US interval (8.5%).
source: and 23 cells showed at least 5 Hz suppression (8.5%, Figure 1D,G,J)
evidence: The claim reports a specific count and percentage of cells showing suppression, with reference to figure panels.

claim: 187 cells did not show any clear spike rate modulation within the CS-US interval (69.3%).
source: leaving 187 cells that did not show any clear spike rate modulation within the CS-US interval (69.3%, Figure 1E,H,K; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim reports a specific count and percentage of cells without modulation, with reference to figure panels.

claim: CRs were present in at least 20% of trials in 103 cells (38%).
source: In terms of eyelid behavior across the dataset (Figure 1L), CRs were present in at least 20% of trials in 103 cells (38%)
evidence: The claim reports the prevalence of conditioned responses across the dataset.

claim: The magnitude of spike facilitation showed a steady significant increase over the course of conditioning.
source: The magnitude of spike facilitation showed a steady significant increase over the course of conditioning (r = 0.413, p=0.001, n = 60; Spearman)
evidence: The claim reports a correlation with statistical significance indicating an increase over time.

claim: Both facilitation and suppression manifested before conditioned behavior did.
source: Although both types of spike rate modulation manifested before conditioned behavior did (Figure 1M)
evidence: The claim describes the temporal relationship between spike modulation and behavior, with reference to a figure.

claim: Facilitation was more prevalent in recordings with conditioned behavior (29.1%) than in those without (18%).
source: they were more prevalent in recordings with conditioned behavior (Figure 1O) than in those without (Figure 1N; facilitation: 29.1% (30/103) vs. 18% (30/167), p=0.0463
evidence: The claim reports a statistical comparison of facilitation prevalence between two groups.

claim: Suppression was more prevalent in recordings with conditioned behavior (15.5%) than in those without (4.2%).
source: suppression: 15.5% (16/103) vs. 4.2% (7/167), p=0.0025, Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim reports a statistical comparison of suppression prevalence between two groups.

claim: The second dataset was collected after thorough training, and only from mice that showed at least 80% CRs.
source: The collection of this dataset was optimized in that: (i) rather than over the course of conditioning, these recordings were obtained after thorough training, and only from mice that showed at least 80% CRs
evidence: The claim describes the specific criteria for data collection in the second dataset.

claim: The recordings in the second dataset were all located no more than ~300 μm away from IpN sites confirmed to be eyelid-related through micro-stimulation.
source: (ii) the recordings were all located no more than ~300 μm away from IpN sites confirmed to be eyelid-related through micro-stimulation (see Materials and methods, and Heiney et al., 2014b)
evidence: The claim describes the spatial criteria for recordings in the second dataset, with citation.

claim: In the second dataset, the CS was 220 ms, the US was 20 ms, resulting in a CS-US interval of 200 ms.
source: and (iii) the CS was 220 ms, the US was 20 ms, resulting in a CS-US interval of 200 ms.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental parameters used in the second dataset.

claim: Out of 30 facilitation cells recorded in the presence of CRs, 17 showed significant positive trial-by-trial correlations between firing rate and CR amplitude (57%).
source: Out of 30 facilitation cells recorded in the presence of CRs (Figure 2A), 17 showed significant positive trial-by-trial correlations between firing rate and CR amplitude (57%; p=0.0001, bootstrap with 500 repetitions; Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim reports a statistical finding about correlations between neural activity and behavior.

claim: A linear mixed model predicts 0.49% more eyelid closure at US onset per unit increase of spike facilitation in Hz.
source: A linear mixed model with random intercepts and slopes for these significant cells predicts 0.49% more eyelid closure at US onset per unit increase of spike facilitation in Hz (Figure 2B, black dotted line; p<0.0001, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim reports the result of a statistical model relating neural activity to behavior.

claim: Spike facilitation fits best with subsequent eyelid behavior, averaging 25 ± 25.6 ms.
source: Indeed, temporal cross-correlations between average spike and eyelid traces confirmed that spike facilitation fits best with subsequent eyelid behavior, averaging 25 ± 25.6 ms (p=0.0001, Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior with statistical support.

claim: In the second dataset, 70 cells showed facilitation (59.2 ± 38 Hz) in the presence of conditioned behavior.
source: The character and predictive power of CS-US facilitation in the IpN was corroborated by the second dataset (Figure 2E–H), with 70 cells showing facilitation (59.2 ± 38 Hz) in the presence of conditioned behavior (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim reports findings from the second dataset that corroborate the first dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, 49 of 70 facilitation cells showed significant positive correlations (70%).
source: and 49 of these cells showing significant positive correlations (70%).
evidence: The claim reports the proportion of cells showing significant correlations in the second dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, a linear mixed model predicted 0.64% more eyelid closure at US onset per 1 Hz increase in facilitation.
source: A linear mixed model with random intercepts and slopes predicted 0.64% more eyelid closure at US onset per 1 Hz increase in facilitation (p<0.0001, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim reports the result of a statistical model in the second dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, temporal cross-correlations confirmed the best fit between spike facilitation and eyelid behavior to be at significantly positive offsets (33.4 ± 19.3 ms).
source: with temporal cross-correlations again confirming the best fit between spike facilitation and eyelid behavior to be at significantly positive offsets (33.4 ± 19.3 ms, p<0.0001, Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal relationship with statistical support from the second dataset.

claim: In the first dataset, 23 cells (8.5%) showed an average drop of at least 5 Hz in the CS-US interval.
source: In the first dataset, CS-US suppression was less prevalent than facilitation. Within the 23 cells (8.5%) showing an average drop of at least 5 Hz in the CS-US interval (11.2 ± 6 Hz, duration: 70 ± 44 ms)
evidence: The claim reports the prevalence and characteristics of suppression in the first dataset.

claim: The magnitude of suppression correlated to both CR percentage and CR amplitude at US onset.
source: the magnitude of suppression correlated to both CR percentage (r = 0.526, p=0.01, n = 23, Spearman) and CR amplitude at US onset (r = 0.443, p=0.0356, n = 23, Spearman).
evidence: The claim reports correlations between suppression magnitude and behavioral measures.

claim: Cells with stronger suppression showed higher spike irregularity (i.e., higher CVs).
source: Additionally, cells with stronger suppression showed higher spike irregularity (i.e., higher CVs: r = 0.587, p=0.0038, Spearman).
evidence: The claim reports a correlation between suppression strength and spike irregularity.

claim: Suppression had lower amplitudes than facilitation (baseline z-score: 5.3 ± 1.5 vs 7.6 ± 4.7).
source: Compared to facilitation, suppression had lower amplitudes (baseline z-score: 5.3 ± 1.5 vs 7.6 ± 4.7, p=0.0007, Mann-Whitney U test, MWU)
evidence: The claim reports a statistical comparison between suppression and facilitation amplitudes.

claim: Suppression had lower durations than facilitation (53 ± 38.4 vs 95.5 ± 36.2 ms).
source: and lower durations (53 ± 38.4 vs 95.5 ± 36.2 ms, p=0.0012, MWU)
evidence: The claim reports a statistical comparison between suppression and facilitation durations.

claim: Of 16 suppressive cells with conditioned behavior, three showed significant negative trial-by-trial correlations between firing rate and CR amplitude (19%).
source: Of these cells, three showed significant negative trial-by-trial correlations between firing rate and CR amplitude (19%, p<0.0001, bootstrap with 500 repetitions; Figure 2J)
evidence: The claim reports the proportion of suppressive cells showing significant correlations.

claim: A linear mixed model for suppressive cells estimated 0.27% more eyelid closure at US onset per unitary increase of suppression in Hz.
source: A linear mixed model with random intercepts and slopes for the three significant cells estimated 0.27% more eyelid closure at US onset per unitary increase of suppression in Hz (p=0.0272, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim reports the result of a statistical model for suppressive cells.

claim: Temporal cross-correlation for suppressive cells showed a best fit between average spike and eyelid traces at very small temporal offsets that were on average close to zero (6.4 ± 23 ms).
source: and temporal cross-correlation showed a best fit between average spike and eyelid traces at very small temporal offsets that were on average close to zero (6.4 ± 23 ms, p=0.2336, Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal relationship for suppressive cells with statistical details.

claim: In the second dataset, 16 cells showed CS-US spike suppression (12.1 ± 5 Hz) in the presence of conditioned behavior.
source: In the second dataset, 16 cells showed CS-US spike suppression (12.1 ± 5 Hz) in the presence of conditioned behavior (Figure 2M)
evidence: The claim reports findings about suppression in the second dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, 8 suppressive cells showed a significant negative relationship between relative firing rate and CR amplitude at US onset.
source: with 8 cells showing a significant negative relationship between relative firing rate and CR amplitude at US onset (p<0.0001, bootstrap with 500 repetitions; Figure 2N)
evidence: The claim reports the number of cells showing significant correlations in the second dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, a linear mixed model for suppressive cells estimated 1.01% more eyelid closure per 1 Hz deeper suppression.
source: and a linear mixed model estimating 1.01% more eyelid closure per 1 Hz deeper suppression (p<0.0001, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim reports the result of a statistical model for suppressive cells in the second dataset.

claim: The second dataset showed stronger facilitation than the first dataset (59.2 ± 38.1 vs 30.1 ± 25.3 Hz).
source: Although the second dataset showed stronger facilitation than the first dataset (59.2 ± 38.1 vs 30.1 ± 25.3 Hz, p=0.0009, MWU), arguably due to superior CR performance (mean percentage CRs: 86.2 ± 17.3%; mean CR amplitude: 43.5 ± 17% eyelid closure)
evidence: The claim reports a comparison between the two datasets with statistical support.

claim: The level of suppression was not different between the two datasets (11.9 ± 5 Hz vs 12.9 ± 6.4 Hz).
source: the level of suppression was not different between the two datasets (11.9 ± 5 Hz vs 12.9 ± 6.4 Hz, p=0.864, MWU).
evidence: The claim reports a comparison showing no significant difference between datasets.

claim: In the second dataset, the time difference between suppressive modulation and eyelid movement was not significantly different from zero on average (6.9 ± 25 ms).
source: Moreover, the correlation matrices for eyelid position (Figure 2O) and velocity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) echo-ed the finding that the time difference between suppressive modulation and eyelid movement was not significantly different from zero on average (6.9 ± 25 ms, p=0.2439, Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 2P).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal relationship with statistical support from the second dataset.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of IpN during the CS-US interval abolished CRs in all three mice.
source: Indeed, the conditioned behavior acquired by all three mice was readily disabled in virtually all trials randomly chosen to include optogenetic stimulation (all p<0.0001, MWU; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim reports the result of an optogenetic manipulation experiment with statistical support.

claim: IpN facilitation is decidedly necessary for the expression of conditioned eyelid responses.
source: This result expands on the observation that IpN facilitation can elicit eyeblinks (Hesslow, 1994b; Heiney et al., 2014b), by showing that it is decidedly necessary for the expression of conditioned eyelid responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by the optogenetic experiment and citations to prior work.

claim: Seven cells showed a striking transient suppression at 88 ± 12 ms, referred to as a CS pause.
source: Seven cells showed a striking transient suppression at 88 ± 12 ms (Figure 4B,E), which we refer to as a CS pause
evidence: The claim reports the observation of a specific neural response pattern.

claim: Five of seven cells showing a CS pause also showed subsequent facilitation in the CS-US interval (71.4%).
source: with five of them showing a subsequent facilitation in the CS-US interval (71.4%, vs 55/263 (21%), p=0.0006, Fisher's test).
evidence: The claim reports a statistical association between CS pause and facilitation.

claim: In the second dataset, 41 out of 102 cells showed CS pauses.
source: The presence and character of CS pauses as observed in the first dataset were strongly reflected in the second dataset, which was obtained from fully trained, high-performing mice. Out of 102 cells, 41 showed CS pauses (Figure 4C,F)
evidence: The claim reports the prevalence of CS pauses in the second dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, cells with a CS pause were more likely to show CS-US facilitation (95%) than those without (51%).
source: and here too cells with a CS pause were more likely to show CS-US facilitation than those without (39/41 (95%) vs 31/61 (51%) cells, p<0.0001, Fisher's test).
evidence: The claim reports a statistical association between CS pause and facilitation in the second dataset.

claim: There was a clear across-cell correlation between average CS pause latency and CR latency.
source: Importantly, there was a clear across-cell correlation between average CS pause latency and CR latency, whether looking at both datasets combined (n = 45, r = 0.582, p<0.0001, Pearson; Figure 4G), or just the second dataset in isolation (n = 41, r = 0.403, p=0.0089, Pearson).
evidence: The claim reports a correlation between neural response timing and behavioral timing.

claim: Four cells in the first dataset showed a transient increase, rather than a decrease, in firing at the same latency as the CS pause.
source: Interestingly, there were four cells in the first dataset that showed a transient increase, rather than a decrease, in firing at the same latency as the CS pause (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim reports an observation of a different response pattern in a subset of cells.

claim: None of the 11 cells showing a transient spike response at the CS-related complex spike latency were recorded before day 4 of training.
source: Across the first dataset, which was obtained over the course of conditioning, none of the 11 cells showing a transient spike response (CS pause or a transient increase in spikes) at the CS-related complex spike latency were recorded before day 4 of training (day 1–3, 0/99 cells; day 4+, 11/171, p=0.0058, Fisher's test; Figure 4H)
evidence: The claim reports a temporal pattern in the emergence of CS-related responses during training.

claim: Cells with CS pauses showed significantly higher CR-related increases in firing rate during the CS-US interval (41.5 ± 33.1 vs 15.2 ± 8.9 Hz) in the first dataset.
source: In the first dataset, they showed significantly higher CR-related increases in firing rate during the CS-US interval (41.5 ± 33.1 vs 15.2 ± 8.9 Hz, p=0.0013, MWU; Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim reports a statistical comparison between cells with and without CS pauses.

claim: Cells with CS pauses showed distinctly higher maximum spike rate velocities (4.9 ± 1.6 vs 1.4 ± 0.5 Hz/ms) in the first dataset.
source: and they also showed distinctly higher maximum spike rate velocities (4.9 ± 1.6 vs 1.4 ± 0.5 Hz/ms, p=0.0002, MWU; Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim reports a statistical comparison of spike rate velocities between cell groups.

claim: In the second dataset, cells with CS pauses showed significantly higher maximum spike rate velocities (5.6 ± 2.5 vs 3.6 ± 1.5 Hz/ms).
source: While in the second dataset maximum facilitation was not significantly higher in facilitation cells with a CS pause (65.1 ± 39.5 Hz) compared to those without (51.7 ± 35.4 Hz, p=0.1594, MWU; Figure 5H), the former group did show significantly higher maximum spike rate velocities (5.6 ± 2.5 vs 3.6 ± 1.5 Hz/ms, p=0.0004, MWU; Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim reports a statistical comparison in the second dataset.

claim: CS pause cells tended to be recorded less deeply in the nuclei than non-CS pause cells in both datasets.
source: Note that CS pause cells tended to be recorded less deeply in the nuclei than non-CS pause cells, in both the first (1840 ± 320 vs 2130 ± 350 μm, p=0.0298, MWU; Figure 5E) and second dataset (2350 ± 140 vs 2450 ± 211 μm, p=0.0372, MWU; Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim reports a spatial relationship between cell type and recording depth.

claim: 211 cells of the first dataset (78.2%) showed a marked increase in IpN spikes 10.6 ± 4.7 ms after US onset, referred to as a US peak.
source: Interestingly, 10.6 ± 4.7 ms after US onset we found a marked increase in IpN spikes (99 ± 59 Hz), which exceeded five baseline SDs in 211 cells of the first dataset (78.2%, Figure 6A,B, see Materials and methods). This IpN response, here referred to as a US peak
evidence: The claim reports the observation and prevalence of a US-related response.

claim: US peak amplitude diminished over the course of training (88 ± 48 vs. 29 ± 44 Hz).
source: First, US peak amplitude, measured from baseline, diminished over the course of training, as apparent from a comparison of recordings made in the first four training days and those made subsequently (88 ± 48 vs. 29 ± 44 Hz, p<0.0001, MWU; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal change in US peak amplitude with statistical support.

claim: US peak amplitude correlated negatively with conditioned behavior, in terms of both CR percentage and CR amplitude at US onset.
source: Second, US peak amplitude correlated negatively with conditioned behavior, in terms of both CR percentage (r = −0.426, p<0.0001, n = 270, Spearman) and CR amplitude at US onset (r = −0.333, p<0.0001, n = 270, Spearman), confirming its reduction as conditioned behavior is acquired.
evidence: The claim reports correlations between US peak amplitude and behavioral measures.

claim: Among 62 recordings with a US peak and CR behavior, 13 cells showed negative trial-by-trial correlations between US peak amplitude and CR amplitude.
source: Furthermore, among 62 recordings with a US peak and CR behavior, trial-by-trial correlations revealed 13 cells in which US peak amplitude correlated negatively to CR amplitude (p<0.0001, bootstrap with 500 repetitions; Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim reports trial-by-trial correlations with statistical support.

claim: Cells showing significant positive correlations between CR amplitude and CS-US facilitation were twice as likely to also show US peaks.
source: These significant recordings were twice as likely as the other 49 cells to also show significant positive correlations between CR amplitude and CS-US facilitation (69.2% (9/13) versus 36.7% (18/49), p=0.0077, Fisher test)
evidence: The claim reports a statistical association between different neural response features.

claim: CS-US facilitation was three times as likely to occur in cells with US peak compared to those without.
source: which itself was three times as likely to occur in cells with US peak compared to those without (26.1% (55/211) vs. 5/59, 8.5% (5/59), p=0.007, Fisher test).
evidence: The claim reports a statistical association between US peak and CS-US facilitation.

claim: 105 IpN cells (39%) showed transient suppressive responses at 28.2 ± 4.9 ms post-US, referred to as the US pause.
source: In addition to US peak responses, transient suppressive responses were also observed at 28.2 ± 4.9 ms post-US in 105 IpN cells (39%), with mean magnitudes of −50 ± 24 Hz (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim reports the observation and prevalence of US pause responses.

claim: The majority of cells that showed a CS pause also showed a US pause (86%).
source: Consistent with this notion, the majority of cells that showed a CS pause also showed a US pause (86%, vs. 105/263 (40%), p=0.0012, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The claim reports a statistical association between CS pause and US pause.

claim: A third of the cells showing US peak or US pause also showed the other response (77 out of 239, 32.2%).
source: We found considerable overlap in the prevalence of US peaks and pauses: a third of the cells showing the one response also showed the other (77 out of 239, 32.2%; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim reports the co-occurrence of US peak and US pause responses.

claim: Cells with only a US pause tended to be more dorsally located (1939 ± 299 μm) than cells with only a US peak (2182 ± 373 μm).
source: Additionally, cells with only a US pause tended to be more dorsally located (1939 ± 299 μm) than cells with only a US peak (2182 ± 373 μm), and cells that showed both responses averaged an intermediate depth (2075 ± 322 μm; p=0.0025, Kruskal-Wallis; Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim reports a spatial relationship between cell response types and recording depth.

claim: Across the first four training days, 47.1% of cells showed a US pause, compared to 30% on subsequent training days.
source: Across the first four training days, 47.1% of cells (66/140) showed a US pause, compared to 30% (39/130) on subsequent training days in the first dataset (p=0.0057, Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal change in US pause prevalence with statistical support.

claim: Further into training (day 5+), the US pause showed lower magnitudes than those observed on earlier days (−13 ± 30.3 vs −28.8 ± 30.4 Hz).
source: Moreover, further into training (day 5+), the US pause showed lower magnitudes than those observed on earlier days (−13 ± 30.3 vs −28.8 ± 30.4 Hz, resp., p=0.0018, MWU).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal change in US pause magnitude with statistical support.

claim: On a trial-by-trial basis, 4 out of 41 recordings with a US pause and at least 20% CRs showed deeper pauses in trials with worse behavior.
source: Furthermore, on a trial-by-trial basis, 4 out of 41 recordings with a US pause and at least 20% CRs showed deeper pauses in trials with worse behavior (p=0.0017, bootstrap with 500 repetitions; Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim reports trial-by-trial correlations with statistical support.

claim: US pauses were observed less frequently in the second dataset (23.5%).
source: Note that, as with the US peak, US pauses were observed less frequently in the second dataset (23.5%).
evidence: The claim reports a difference in US pause prevalence between datasets.

claim: 83 IpN cells in the first dataset showed a rapid excitatory response that peaked at 46 ± 7 ms with magnitudes of 61.4 ± 28.3 Hz (39.4%), referred to as the second US peak.
source: In addition to the US peak and pause responses, 83 IpN cells in the first dataset showed a rapid excitatory response that peaked at 46 ± 7 ms and showed magnitudes of 61.4 ± 28.3 Hz (39.4%; Figure 7A, arrow), which we refer to as the second US peak.
evidence: The claim reports the observation and characteristics of a second US peak response.

claim: The second US peak was more prevalent in recordings with poor conditioned behavior (26 ± 32 Hz, vs 13 ± 26 Hz).
source: Like the first US peak, the second peak was more prevalent in recordings with poor conditioned behavior (26 ± 32 Hz, vs 13 ± 26 Hz, p=0.025, MWU; Figure 7E)
evidence: The claim reports a relationship between second US peak and behavioral performance.

claim: The second US peak did not show a steady decline over the course of training days.
source: but it did not show a steady decline over the course of training days (r = 0.102, p=0.13, n = 224, Spearman).
evidence: The claim reports the absence of a temporal trend with statistical support.

claim: Across recordings in which CR performance was poor, the second US peak actually grew stronger over the course of conditioning days.
source: To the contrary, across recordings in which CR performance was poor, the second US peak actually grew stronger over the course of conditioning days (r = 0.287, p=0.0007, n = 138, Spearman), with maximum peak amplitudes 30–60 ms post-US of 16 ± 28.3 Hz on training days 1–4 (n = 121), and 46.5 ± 33 Hz on later training days (n = 46, p=0.0001, MWU; Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal change in second US peak amplitude with statistical support.

claim: Spike rate velocity was lower during the second US peak on earlier training days compared to later ones (0.55 ± 0.32 vs 0.77 ± 0.45 Hz/ms).
source: Similarly, spike rate velocity was lower during the second US peak on earlier training days compared to later ones (0.55 ± 0.32 vs 0.77 ± 0.45 Hz/ms, p=0.0072, MWU; Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim reports a temporal change in spike rate velocity with statistical support.

claim: In the second dataset, only 9 cells (8.8%) showed a first US peak response.
source: Consistent with the observation that US-related responses in IpN neurons tended to occur during recordings in which CR performance was poor (Figure 6; Figure 7E), we found that in the second dataset (in which CR performance was very high) only 9 cells (8.8%) showed a first US peak response
evidence: The claim reports the prevalence of first US peak in the second dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, only 24 cells (23.5%) showed a US pause.
source: only 24 (23.5%) showed a US pause
evidence: The claim reports the prevalence of US pause in the second dataset.

claim: In the second dataset, only 11 cells (10.8%) showed a second US peak.
source: and only 11 (10.8%) showed a second US peak (CR amplitude: 31.3 ± 15.9 vs 44.9 ± 16.6% eyelid closure, p=0.021, MWU; Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim reports the prevalence of second US peak in the second dataset with behavioral comparison.

claim: In US-only trials, both the first US peak (10/25 cells, 40%) and US pause (10/25, 40%) showed a higher prevalence than in paired trials.
source: Indeed, both the first US peak (10/25 cells, 40%) and US pause (10/25, 40%) showed a higher prevalence in US-only trials than in paired trials
evidence: The claim reports a comparison of response prevalence between trial types.

claim: The second US peak was the most substantial in US-only trials, occurring in 18 cells (72%), and outranking the first US peak in terms of amplitude (94.6 ± 82.9 vs 27.8 ± 48.7 Hz).
source: but the second US peak was the most substantial, occurring in 18 cells (72%), and outranking the first US peak in terms of amplitude (94.6 ± 82.9 vs 27.8 ± 48.7 Hz, p=0.0012, MWU).
evidence: The claim reports a comparison of US peak responses in US-only trials.

claim: There was a remarkable similarity between the pause and subsequent rapid excitation observed after the US in US-only trials, and the pause and subsequent rapid excitation observed after the CS in paired trials.
source: In fact, there was a remarkable similarity between the pause and subsequent rapid excitation observed after the US in US-only trials, and the pause and subsequent rapid excitation observed after the CS in paired trials (Figure 7F,G), hinting at the possibility of a similar underlying mechanism.
evidence: The claim reports an observation suggesting a common mechanism, with reference to figures.

claim: Trial-by-trial correlations and their temporal distribution, as well as optogenetic abolition of CRs, evince and characterize the causal relation between IpN facilitation and conditioned eyelid-behavior.
source: Trial-by-trial correlations and their temporal distribution across the trial timespan, as well as optogenetic abolition of CRs, evince and characterize the causal relation between IpN facilitation and conditioned eyelid-behavior.
evidence: The claim summarizes the evidence supporting a causal relationship between IpN activity and behavior.

claim: The dynamic modulation of activity in the IpN during the generation of conditioned eyelid movements can be affected through a learned Purkinje cell simple spike suppression.
source: The data suggest that the dynamic modulation of activity in the IpN during the generation of conditioned eyelid movements can be affected through a learned Purkinje cell simple spike suppression on the one hand, and through climbing fiber mediated Purkinje cell complex spike activity, possibly in tandem with activation of mossy fiber and climbing fiber collaterals, on the other (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim presents an interpretation of the data regarding mechanisms of IpN modulation.

claim: The dynamic modulation of activity in the IpN during the generation of conditioned eyelid movements can be affected through climbing fiber mediated Purkinje cell complex spike activity, possibly in tandem with activation of mossy fiber and climbing fiber collaterals.
source: The data suggest that the dynamic modulation of activity in the IpN during the generation of conditioned eyelid movements can be affected through a learned Purkinje cell simple spike suppression on the one hand, and through climbing fiber mediated Purkinje cell complex spike activity, possibly in tandem with activation of mossy fiber and climbing fiber collaterals, on the other (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim presents an interpretation of the data regarding mechanisms of IpN modulation.

claim: About one third of the US-responding cells recorded across the IpN over the course of conditioning showed a significant change in spiking activity within the CS-US interval.
source: About one third of the US-responding cells recorded across the IpN over the course of conditioning showed a significant change in spiking activity within the CS-US interval, with a facilitation to suppression ratio of 2.6 (60:23).
evidence: The claim summarizes the proportion of cells showing CS-US modulation.

claim: In the second dataset, 85% of cells showed CS-US spike modulation, with a facilitation to suppression ratio of 4.1 (70:17).
source: In the second dataset, recording from optimally conditioned mice in eyelid-controlling IpN regions, 85% showed CS-US spike modulation, with a facilitation to suppression ratio of 4.1 (70:17).
evidence: The claim reports the proportion and ratio of modulation types in the second dataset.

claim: Facilitation has been shown to predominate over suppression in previous work.
source: Although facilitation has also been shown to predominate over suppression in previous work (McCormick et al., 1982; Berthier and Moore, 1990; Gould and Steinmetz, 1996; Freeman and Nicholson, 2000; Gruart et al., 2000; Choi and Moore, 2003; Green and Arenos, 2007; Halverson et al., 2010; Heiney et al., 2014b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The comprehensive trial-by-trial correlational analysis confirms the leading nature of facilitation in IpN cells.
source: In all, the comprehensive trial-by-trial correlational analysis reported here confirms the leading nature of facilitation in IpN cells, in terms of the temporal profiles of modulation as well as the temporal distribution of spike-eyelid correlations.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from the correlational analysis.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of Purkinje cells suppresses the activity of cerebellar nuclei neurons.
source: Moreover, optogenetic stimulation of Purkinje cells, which was shown to suppress the activity of cerebellar nuclei neurons (Witter et al., 2013; Canto et al., 2016), effectively abolished CRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and the experimental results.

claim: Activation of IpN via optogenetic suppression of Purkinje cells is sufficient to elicit eyelid behavior.
source: Thus, while it was shown previously that activation of IpN via optogenetic suppression of Purkinje cells is sufficient to elicit eyelid behavior (Heiney et al., 2014a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: IpN neurons showing CR-related suppression of activity have previously been reported and were hypothesized to facilitate conditioned behavior through inactivation of antagonistic muscles.
source: IpN neurons showing CR-related suppression of activity have previously been reported in Berthier and Moore (1990) and Gruart et al., 2000, and were hypothesized to facilitate conditioned behavior through inactivation of antagonistic muscles (Gruart et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The transient IpN spike pauses strikingly mirror the CS- and US-related complex spike responses found in eyelid-related Purkinje cells.
source: The transient IpN spike pauses observed across datasets strikingly mirror the CS- and US-related complex spike responses found in eyelid-related Purkinje cells (Ohmae and Medina, 2015; ten Brinke et al., 2015 and Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and reference to a figure showing the similarity.

claim: The translation from complex spike input to a pause response in the IpN is supported by findings that climbing fiber activation can trigger a prominent inhibition in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: The translation from complex spike input to a pause response in the IpN is supported by the findings that climbing fiber activation can trigger a prominent inhibition in the cerebellar nuclei (Hoebeek et al., 2010; Bengtsson et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism.

claim: The strength of inhibition in the cerebellar nuclei can be related to the synchrony of the complex spikes.
source: and that the strength of this inhibition can be related to the synchrony of the complex spikes (De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on complex spike synchrony.

claim: The excitatory response of IpN neurons is normally attributed to learning-related suppression of Purkinje cell activity, plasticity of the excitatory mossy fiber to IpN connection, or a combination of the two.
source: The excitatory response of IpN neurons is normally attributed to learning-related suppression of Purkinje cell activity, plasticity of the excitatory mossy fiber to IpN connection, or a combination of the two (Medina et al., 2000; Ohyama et al., 2006; Longley and Yeo, 2014; Freeman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on mechanisms of IpN excitation.

claim: The CS-related spike pause is likely to have a direct impact on the subsequent spike modulation.
source: This CS-related spike pause is likely to have a direct impact on the subsequent spike modulation, as the modulation amplitudes and velocity were significantly higher in the cells with a CS-related spike pause (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed relationship between CS pause and subsequent modulation.

claim: The characteristic profile of CS pause followed by strong excitation fits well with the notion of rebound depolarization in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: This characteristic profile fits well with the notion of rebound depolarization in the cerebellar nuclei (Hoebeek et al., 2010; Bengtsson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citations to studies on rebound depolarization.

claim: Rebound depolarization is well established in vitro.
source: This phenomenon is well established in vitro (Jahnsen, 1986; Llinás and Mühlethaler, 1988; Aizenman and Linden, 1999; Tadayonnejad et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: Rebound depolarization can be elicited through electrical and optogenetic stimulation.
source: and can be elicited through electrical (cerebellar nuclei and inferior olive, Hoebeek et al., 2010; inferior olive and skin, Bengtsson et al., 2011) and optogenetic (inferior olive, Lu et al., 2016; cerebellar nuclei, Witter et al., 2013) stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to stimulation studies.

claim: Rebound-driven behavioral responses can be elicited by synchronized nuclear inhibition lasting as little as 25 ms.
source: In particular, rebound-driven behavioral responses can be elicited by synchronized nuclear inhibition lasting as little as 25 ms (Witter et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this effect.

claim: Particularly synchronized complex spike input seems fit to induce substantial rebound excitation in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Bengtsson et al., 2011 and Hoebeek et al. (2010) report that particularly synchronized complex spike input seems fit to induce substantial rebound excitation in the cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on synchronized complex spike input.

claim: There are stimulation studies showing less convincing rebound.
source: Nevertheless, there are also stimulation studies showing less convincing rebound (Chaumont et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study with different findings.

claim: Spontaneous occurrence of rebound in vitro or in vivo seems negligible.
source: and its spontaneous occurrence in vitro or in vivo seems negligible (Alviña et al., 2008; Reato et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on spontaneous rebound.

claim: The data offer some evidence for an affirmative answer to the open question of whether rebound may occur during learning.
source: Given the dependence of several models of cerebellar learning on the ability of the cerebellar nuclei to use rebound depolarization to trigger mechanisms of plasticity (e.g., Kistler et al., 1999; Steuber et al., 2007; Wetmore et al., 2008; De Zeeuw et al., 2011), the data here presented are particularly relevant in that they offer some evidence for an affirmative answer to the open question of whether rebound may occur during learning (Reato et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data in the context of prior models and questions, supported by citations.

claim: The rapid post-US excitatory response had an average latency of 10.6 ms (25th-75th percentile: 7–12 ms).
source: The rapid post-US excitatory response had an average latency of 10.6 ms (25th-75th percentile: 7–12 ms), which allows for both mossy fiber and climbing fiber collateral activation as possible pathways for driving the response (Berthier and Moore, 1990; Cody and Richardson, 1979; Mostofi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim reports a measured latency and interprets it in the context of possible pathways, with citations.

claim: Mostofi et al. (2010) point at latencies < 6 ms for mossy fiber activation as recorded in the cerebellar cortex in awake rabbits in response to peri-ocular electrical stimulation.
source: Mostofi et al. (2010) point at latencies < 6 ms for mossy fiber activation as recorded in the cerebellar cortex in awake rabbits in response to peri-ocular electrical stimulation, and latencies > 9 ms for climbing fiber responses
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study reporting these latencies.

claim: Mossy fiber input may more appropriately fit the observed manifestation of the US peak due to its widespread distribution and robust input to the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Therefore, mossy fiber input, which is not assumed to adhere to such a modular organization and forms a more robust input to the cerebellar nuclei (e.g. Person and Raman, 2010), may more appropriately fit the observed manifestation of the US peak.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the observed distribution of US peaks and known properties of mossy fiber input, with citation.

claim: The reduction of US peak responses over the course of conditioning may reflect the reduced impact of the air puff US due to protection of the eyelid, and a resultant reduced mossy fiber signal.
source: Moreover, the reduction of US peak responses over the course of conditioning may well reflect the reduced impact of the air puff US due to protection of the eyelid, and a resultant reduced mossy fiber signal.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed reduction in US peak responses.

claim: There is research to suggest that climbing fiber collateral input may be more robust than the notion of 'sparse collaterals' suggests.
source: On the other hand, there is research to suggest that climbing fiber collateral input may be more robust (Van der Want et al., 1989; Hesslow, 1994b; De Zeeuw and Yeo, 2005) than the notion of 'sparse collaterals' suggests (Chan-Palay, 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on climbing fiber collaterals.

claim: Stimulation of the inferior olive results in a consistent excitatory response in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Moreover, stimulation of the inferior olive results in a consistent excitatory response in the cerebellar nuclei (Kitai et al., 1977; Hoebeek et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to stimulation studies.

claim: Spontaneous complex spikes elicit a co-occurrence of excitatory and inhibitory responses in the nuclei 24% of the time.
source: and spontaneous complex spikes elicit a co-occurrence of excitatory and inhibitory responses in the nuclei 24% of the time (Blenkinsop and Lang, 2011), which is not very different from the percentage we observed (32%).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and comparison to the observed data.

claim: The cell- and trial-wide correlations suggesting weaker US-peaks with better CRs may be explained in terms of a changing level of nucleo-olivary inhibition.
source: The cell- and trial-wide correlations suggesting weaker US-peaks with better CRs may also be explained in terms of a changing level of nucleo-olivary inhibition (Medina et al., 2002), which would agree with a contribution of the climbing fiber collaterals (De Zeeuw et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The interesting occurrence of weaker US peaks in trials where mice opened their eyes further than baseline agrees with Purkinje cell US-complex spike data.
source: Moreover, the interesting occurrence of weaker US peaks in trials where mice opened their eyes further than baseline, agrees with Purkinje cell US-complex spike data from ten Brinke et al. (2015), underlining another similarity between the US peak and climbing fiber activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and comparison to prior data.

claim: While these arguments suggest it is likely that climbing fibers contribute to the US peak response, its broad prevalence across the IpN suggests mossy fibers are also involved.
source: Thus, while these arguments suggest it is likely that climbing fibers contribute to the US peak response, its broad prevalence across the IpN suggests mossy fibers are also involved.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed distribution and properties of the US peak.

claim: Only a relatively small portion of the IpN neurons might evoke functional behavioral responses, considering the strong convergence of Purkinje cells onto IpN neurons (approx. 40:1).
source: Considering the strong convergence of Purkinje cells onto IpN neurons (approx. 40:1) (Person and Raman, 2011), only a relatively small portion of the IpN neurons might evoke functional behavioral responses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on known convergence ratios, with citation.

claim: The large pool of remaining IpN neurons may show US-responses that relay general sensory information of the face or feed into cognitive processes.
source: As the large pool of remaining IpN neurons may show US-responses that relay general sensory information of the face, including that of the areas surrounding the eyelid region (Koekkoek et al., 2002), or feed into cognitive processes (Wagner et al., 2017; Sokolov et al., 2017), there may also be a substantial amount of redundant, yet detectable, spike responses.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Dense population coding during eyeblink conditioning also occurs at the cerebellar input stage, i.e. in the granule cell layer.
source: This would be consistent with recent findings that dense population coding during eyeblink conditioning also occurs at the cerebellar input stage, i.e. in the granule cell layer (D'Angelo et al., 2009; Giovannucci et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on granule cell layer coding.

source: which may partly result from nucleocortical feedback originating in the IpN (Houck and Person, 2015; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Climbing fiber input to the cerebellar cortex could provide an additional mechanism through which spike modulation may be elicited in the IpN to fine-tune the timing of CRs.

evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: These results underline the relevance of olivary climbing fibers beyond their conventional role of providing teaching signals.
source: These results underline the relevance of olivary climbing fibers beyond their conventional role of providing teaching signals, highlighting a unique attribute of the olivocerebellar system compared to other networks, which generally segregate the signals that are used for inducing plasticity during learning from signals that are used for performance during memory recall.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the findings in the context of cerebellar function.
